entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Uisang (義湘, 625–702 CE) stands as a towering figure in the intellectual and religious history of Silla Korea, credited with the foundational establishment of the Huayan (Korean: Hwaeom) school of Buddhism on the peninsula. His meticulous scholarship and profound spiritual insight solidified Hwaeom as a dominant philosophical and institutional force, profoundly shaping Korean Buddhist thought and influencing statecraft for centuries. As a contemporary and close friend of the equally eminent Wonhyo, Uisang contributed significantly to the vibrant intellectual ferment of a unified Silla, positioning Korean Buddhism as a major contributor to the East Asian spiritual landscape.

Between 661 and 671 CE, Uisang embarked on a transformative journey to Tang China, studying under the renowned Huayan patriarch Zhiyan (知儼) at Mount Zhongnan. During this decade of intense study, he mastered the intricate doctrines of the Avatamsaka Sutra (Huayan jing), particularly its emphasis on the interpenetration and non-obstruction of all phenomena. Upon his return to Silla, Uisang systematically propagated these teachings, establishing ten key monasteries, most notably Buseoksa (浮石寺) in 676 CE, which became a premier center for Hwaeom scholarship. His magnum opus, the *Hwaeom ilseung beopgye-do* (華嚴一乘法界圖, Chart of the One-Vehicle Dharma-Realm of Huayan), a concise diagrammatic summary of Huayan philosophy, became a cornerstone text for Korean Buddhism.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Uisang was instrumental in establishing the Huayan school in Korea, which became a foundational pillar of Korean Buddhist thought and influenced state ideology for centuries, extending its reach to Japan and shaping a distinct East Asian Buddhist tradition.
